inputs.question: How many test cases do slow problems have and what is per-case sandbox time?
inputs.answer: Operators report many test cases; per-case time unknown.

completeness.repository_coverage: Official judging path (workers/judge, services/submission outbox and result application, pkg/kafka, compose files) read end to end; other services not reviewed.

unknowns.subject: Whether one go-judge /run request with several cmds runs them concurrently
unknowns.what_would_resolve_it: go-judge documentation or a staging test

unknowns.subject: Production WORKER_POOL_SIZE, CPU limits and bundle sizes
unknowns.what_would_resolve_it: Deployed env files and host inspection

known: Official jobs use StopOnFirstFailure, forcing batch size 1 (process_judge_job.go:57, go_judge_client.go:74-77)
Bundle limits are 64 MiB zip and 128 MiB extracted (official_loader.go:29-30)
unknown: Test-case count and bundle size distribution
Production worker and sandbox CPU limits
assumed: Problems have many test cases, per the operator report
Production uses the compose defaults for pool size
derived: An accepted submission with N test cases makes N sequential /run calls plus one compile call for compiled languages, from go_judge_client.go:56-120

decision_changing_questions.question: What is the typical wall time of one test-case run in go-judge, and how many test cases do slow problems have?
What are production WORKER_POOL_SIZE and CPU limits, and what is peak submission concurrency?

root_causes.description: Official test cases are executed strictly serially, one sandbox request each, leaving sandbox capacity idle.
Cached testcase bundle is re-verified and re-read on every job instead of once per version.
Worker job concurrency and CPU are configured far below sandbox capacity.
Outbox relay uses fixed-interval polling with synchronous one-at-a-time publish.

findings.problem: Official submissions run test cases one per blocking sandbox request, strictly in sequence; accepted submissions always pay for every case.
findings.performance_principle: Independent units of work should be overlapped when spare capacity exists; an early-exit optimization must not serialize the whole pipeline.

evidence.statement: Batch size is forced to 1 when StopOnFirstFailure is set.
Sequential loop; each iteration makes one blocking POST /run.
Official jobs always set StopOnFirstFailure true.
Sandbox is configured with ES_PARALLELISM=8 but this path keeps one run in flight per job. No runtime evidence exists.

findings.conditions: Problems with many test cases and non-trivial per-run sandbox overhead; assumes the sandbox has idle capacity. Small N or small per-run cost makes the effect small.

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for concurrency, a test-case pool or pipelining in the loop; none found.
Early exit on first failure reduces work for failing submissions but not for accepted ones.
Compiled languages compile once, not per case.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: If the sandbox is CPU-bound by one job or the host is small, parallelizing one job only shifts load; serial runs also protect timing fairness.
findings.recommendation: Run test cases in windows of K (at or below sandbox parallelism, tuned by measurement), stop issuing windows after the first non-ACCEPTED result, and keep results ordered by index.

alternatives.why: Keeps early exit and uses idle sandbox capacity.

alternatives.option: Keep serial and reduce per-call overhead
alternatives.why: Does not remove the N-fold sandbox launch cost.
Raises throughput across jobs but does not shorten one job.

findings.trade_offs: Up to K-1 wasted runs after a failure; possible CPU-time noise from concurrent execution; more complex result ordering.

validation.metric: End-to-end judge time per job versus test_count for accepted submissions
validation.expectation: Judge time falls for accepted submissions with many cases, bounded by sandbox parallelism and CPU; magnitude not claimed.
validation.falsifier: Per-job time unchanged because the sandbox is CPU-saturated or per-case time is dominated by program runtime; or time-limit verdicts flip.
validation.guard: Benchmark replaying one problem with N cases and a verdict-stability test.

findings.problem: Every job, even on a warm cache, hashes the whole cached zip and re-reads all testcase files; metadata is also fetched per job.
findings.performance_principle: Work whose result is invariant between requests should be validated once, not per request.

evidence.statement: Cache hit still runs verifiedCachedChecksum, which SHA-256s the entire zip.
bundleFromDir re-reads every input and output file on each call.
Metadata fetched over gRPC on each job with no cache. No runtime evidence exists.

findings.conditions: Large bundles (limits allow 64 MiB zip, 128 MiB extracted; actual sizes unknown) or CPU-constrained worker (0.5 CPU in dev compose).

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for an in-memory cache keyed by problem and version; none found.
Hash check is a deliberate integrity guard for the shared volume.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: With bundles of a few MiB, the page cache makes the work cheap relative to running N sandbox processes.
findings.recommendation: Verify the checksum once per (problem, version) per process and keep parsed test cases in a bounded in-memory cache, invalidated on version change.

alternatives.option: Bounded in-memory cache keyed by problem, version and checksum
alternatives.why: Removes disk and hash work from the hot path.

alternatives.option: Verify checksum on first load and on error only

alternatives.why: Acceptable only if bundles are small.

findings.trade_offs: Memory held by the cache and weaker detection of volume corruption between verifications.

validation.metric: Loader duration by cache hit, and bundle sizes on disk
validation.expectation: Load stage time drops on hits.
validation.falsifier: Bundles are small and load time is a negligible share of job time.
validation.guard: Metric on loader duration by hit or miss.

commands.purpose: Find actual cached bundle sizes on the worker host

findings.problem: A shared semaphore limits in-flight jobs per worker; compose defaults it to 1 with a 0.5 CPU dev worker while the sandbox has 2 CPU and parallelism 8, so concurrent submissions queue.
findings.performance_principle: A concurrency limit on a shared resource should match the capacity of the bottleneck resource.

evidence.statement: Pool size comes from WORKER_POOL_SIZE and is enforced by jobSlots.
Production compose defaults WORKER_POOL_SIZE to 1. No runtime evidence exists.

findings.conditions: More than one submission in flight (contests, classes) with idle sandbox CPU; production overrides unknown, compose defaults assumed.

counter_evidence.statement: The limit may be deliberate to keep timing stable on a small host; it is configurable by env var.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: At low submission rates the queue is empty and only per-job time matters; a low value may protect timing accuracy.
findings.recommendation: After PERF-001, measure sandbox and worker CPU under concurrent jobs and set slots and the worker CPU limit accordingly.

alternatives.option: Tune WORKER_POOL_SIZE and CPU from measurements

alternatives.why: Requires locking of the shared testcase cache.

findings.trade_offs: More concurrent runs can perturb CPU-time measurements and raise memory; replicas need cache coordination.

validation.metric: Worker and sandbox CPU and queue wait under several concurrent submissions
validation.expectation: If CPU is mostly idle, queue wait falls with more slots.
validation.falsifier: CPU is already saturated at one job.

commands.purpose: Observe CPU headroom while several submissions run

findings.problem: The outbox relay polls on a fixed 2 s ticker and publishes messages one at a time synchronously, adding up to the poll interval to every submission before it reaches Kafka.
findings.performance_principle: Fixed-interval polling adds latency proportional to the interval to every item on the critical path.

evidence.statement: Relay started with a 2 s poll interval.
Ticker loop and per-message synchronous SendMessage. No runtime evidence exists.

findings.conditions: Constant per submission; independent of test-case count, so it does not explain slowness that grows with test cases.

counter_evidence.statement: Batch of up to 100 pending rows per poll bounds backlog; no per-submission cost beyond the interval was found.

findings.recommendation: If submit-to-start latency matters, shorten the interval or trigger the relay after commit; otherwise leave as is.
findings.trade_offs: More frequent polling adds idle database queries.

validation.metric: Time from submission creation to Kafka publish
validation.expectation: Bounded by the poll interval today.
validation.falsifier: Measured submit-to-publish time is far below the interval.

considered_not_reported.observation: Result persistence could be per-test-case queries
considered_not_reported.why_discarded: One batch Create for all rows inside a single transaction; no N+1 found.
considered_not_reported.revisit_when: Result rows carry large outputs and transaction time shows in Postgres stats.

considered_not_reported.observation: Official runs ignore per-problem limits and use default 2 s CPU and 256 MiB per case
considered_not_reported.why_discarded: Bounded per case and not a source of growth.

adjacent_findings.problem: Testcase cache refresh does RemoveAll then Rename without an inter-process lock; a concurrent reader on the shared volume could see a missing directory.

evidence.statement: Remove and rename sequence with no lock; docs also flag it for multi-replica use.

adjacent_findings.recommendation: Use a per-problem lock or swap through versioned directory names.
adjacent_findings.assessed_properly_by: A correctness-focused test pass if multiple worker replicas are planned.
